record.title: FrontierPhysics benchmarks end-to-end AI-agent research across nine physics domains
record.summary: A 4 November arXiv preprint introduces FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark built from physicists’ own research projects. The authors report 56 tasks from 42 physicists across nine domains, with agents required to plan research, run analyses or experiments, and produce verifiable outputs and manuscripts. Across 22 models and 26 configurations, they report pass rates below 30%; Claude Opus 5.5 is highest at 27.4%. The authors also report manually correcting nine false failures among 168 GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts. These are paper-reported results, not an independent rerun.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors submitted the v1 preprint “FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research” to arXiv on 4 November 2026.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports 56 end-to-end physics-research tasks contributed by 42 physicists across nine domains and evaluates 22 models in 26 configurations. It reports that no configuration passed more than 46 of 168 rollouts; in the main text the highest Pass@1 is 27.4% for Claude Opus 5.5. The authors report manually correcting nine false failures among 168 GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts, changing its pass rate from 25/168 (14.9%) to 34/168 (20.2%).

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected preprint does not independently establish that its task set or pass-rate estimates generalize to scientific research outside the sampled physics projects; this activation did not reproduce the evaluation or inspect raw task and trajectory artifacts.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or external audit of the task set, rubric judgments or model pass rates was inspected.
Although the paper says workspace and trajectory files are collected for Hugging Face datasets, this activation did not identify or inspect the corresponding public dataset and code release.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported evaluation is sound, a multi-domain benchmark built from active physicists’ own open-ended research could materially change how scientific-agent capability is measured and expose the gap between task correctness and publishable research. The score reflects that consequence, not confidence in the paper’s results.
limitations: All benchmark performance numbers are author-reported in an arXiv preprint and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
The same reviewer model, GPT-5.6 Sol, graded all rollouts; the paper reports a Claude Opus 5.5 regrade was more lenient on its own model family.
The paper reports nine false failures corrected during manual review of GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts, showing that the benchmark’s error rate and pass counts are sensitive to evaluation review.
This physics task sample does not establish performance on other scientific disciplines or real-world research programs.
brief.summary: A 4 November arXiv preprint introduces FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark built from physicists’ own research projects. The authors report 56 tasks from 42 physicists across nine domains, with agents required to plan research, run analyses or experiments, and produce verifiable outputs and manuscripts. Across 22 models and 26 configurations, they report pass rates below 30%; Claude Opus 5.5 is highest at 27.4%. The authors also report manually correcting nine false failures among 168 GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts. These are paper-reported results, not an independent rerun.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 56 end-to-end tasks from 42 physicists across nine physics domains; evaluation of 22 models in 26 configurations; highest Pass@1 of 27.4% for Claude Opus 5.5; and a corrected 20.2% pass rate (34/168) for GPT-6 Astra xhigh after manual correction of nine false failures.
technical.compute_or_cost: Appendix G, Table 10 reports mean inference cost per rollout of $26.95 for Claude Opus 5.5 (27.4% pass rate), $19.21 for GPT-6 Astra xhigh (20.2% after the paper's manual false-failure correction), and $3.46 for GPT-6.1 Terra (14.3%). These are paper-reported metered/list-price-derived or estimated inference costs; the table excludes environment setup, verification and rubric review, and does not establish total economic cost or a matched deployment comparison.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv submission and the paper’s reported methods and results are verified as published claims. No benchmark outcome was independently reproduced here.
technical.mechanism: Each task begins from an open research prompt based on a contributor’s own project. Agents must investigate literature, plan and conduct research, and produce numerical artifacts plus a manuscript. The benchmark combines deterministic verifiers with task-specific expert rubrics; failure analysis includes manual review.
technical.regime: Physics only: 56 tasks across nine domains; 22 models in 26 configurations; three trials per model-task and a 10-hour timeout cap per rollout. The study uses different agent harnesses and shared reviewer settings as described by the authors.
technical.reproducibility: The paper says workspace and trajectory artifacts were collected for Hugging Face datasets, but this review did not identify the exact task/rubric/trajectory dataset or rerun the evaluation. Table 10's cost accounting uses metered, list-price-derived or estimated inference cost and is not a full-cost audit.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares its benchmark design with earlier physics and scientific-agent benchmarks; results are within its own FrontierPhysics v0.1 tasks and should not be treated as a matched universal capability ranking.

brief.title: FrontierPhysics benchmarks end-to-end AI-agent research across nine physics domains
brief.why_it_matters: The benchmark tests whether agents can carry a multi-stage research project through to a correct, defensible manuscript, rather than solve a fixed problem or reproduce a supplied paper. If its task curation and grading prove robust, it could sharpen capability comparisons and expose where agents still need expert judgment. The current evidence supports reporting the benchmark and its authors’ results, not a general conclusion that today’s agents can or cannot perform scientific research.
